query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, rapid solidification produces a homogeneous metastable solid solution in which Mg is uniformly dissolved. Upon subsequent thermal exposure, Mg segregates and nucleates as intermetallic compounds at preferred sites (e.g., grain boundaries), which then act to modify local chemistry by promoting the formation of protective oxide layers, thereby altering corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: Rapidly solidified, homogeneous metastable solid solution with uniformly dissolved Mg.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the alloy to controlled thermal aging (annealing at a moderate elevated temperature below full equilibrium transformation limits).
generation.conditions: A controlled comparison between non-aged (baseline) samples and thermally aged samples under identical atmospheric and corrosion test conditions, with the density maintained below 6 g/cm³.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized Mg-rich intermetallic compounds forming during thermal exposure.
generation.mechanism: Thermal aging induces the exsolution of Mg from the solid solution, leading to the nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic phases. These phases either modify the electrochemical characteristics at the alloy surface or catalyze the formation of a protective oxide scale at high temperatures, resulting in enhanced passivation in corrosive environments and improved oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Thermally aged samples will display a microstructure characterized by the presence of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds and exhibit lower corrosion rates and a more stable, protective oxide layer at high temperature compared to the baseline non-aged samples.
generation.baseline: Non-aged rapidly solidified alloy retaining the initial homogeneous metastable state.
generation.boundary: The alloy's processing and testing conditions are limited to a density below 6 g/cm³ and thermal aging conditions that do not lead to full equilibrium decomposition, ensuring that the microstructure remains within the intended non-equilibrium regime.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the precise kinetics of Mg segregation and intermetallic nucleation, and how these microstructural changes quantitatively relate to the observed shifts in corrosion and oxidation properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy samples using rapid solidification. One set will be maintained in the as-solidified state (baseline) and the other subjected to a prescribed thermal aging treatment. Both sets will then be analyzed by microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM and XRD) and tested for corrosion (using standard electrochemical tests) and high-temperature oxidation (via weight gain measurements under controlled temperature conditions).
measurements: Quantitative phase analysis (XRD) to identify formation of Mg-rich intermetallics
High-resolution microstructural imaging (SEM/TEM) to map spatial distribution of phases
Electrochemical corrosion rate measurements (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged alloys do not exhibit a statistically significant difference in microstructure (i.e., absence of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds) or if there is no measurable improvement in corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation performance relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis that Mg segregation and intermetallic formation control these functional properties would be falsified.

recalled_precedents.approach: Rapid solidification was used to produce non‐equilibrium microstructures in Al–Mg alloys. Detailed microscopic and diffraction analyses were performed to follow the evolution from metastable solid solutions toward stable intermetallic phases during subsequent thermal treatments.
recalled_precedents.finding: It was found that metastable states trapped during rapid processing could later transform into stable intermetallic compounds, thereby significantly altering mechanical properties.

recalled_precedents.finding: The study revealed that variations in local chemistry lead to distinct phase assemblages that can cause different corrosion behaviors, highlighting the influence of microstructural evolution on surface reactivity.

recalled_precedents.study: AlMgₓTiSnZn Alloys and Mg-Driven Phase Stability
recalled_precedents.approach: Systematic variation of Mg content was combined with controlled thermal exposures. Advanced structural techniques (XRD, TEM) and functional testing (hardness and oxidation resistance evaluations) were used to monitor phase stability and property evolution.
recalled_precedents.finding: Higher Mg levels were correlated with the stabilization of certain phases, which in turn modified oxidation kinetics and other functional behaviors, suggesting that Mg-induced microstructural changes are key to performance.
